candidates.statement: In the absence of availability of a dosage form that is appropriate for the targeted patient 57 population (e.g., pediatric, geriatric), small amounts of liquids and/or soft foods as described in 58 the FDA-approved product labeling can be used as a suitable vehicle(s) for oral administration 59 and immediate ingestion of the specific drug product. Generally, drug products mixed in small 60 amounts of liquids (5 to 15 mL) or soft foods are used in pediatric and other patient populations 61 who are unable to swallow solid oral dosage forms. Although sponsors are required to develop 62 age-appropriate formulations as part of a pediatric drug development program 7 occasionally the 63 development of age-appropriate dosage forms and formulations proves to be exceedingly 64 complex. The use of a liquid such as infant formula or breast milk and/or soft food as a 65 vehicle(s) may be the only option for delivering the drug substance to the targeted patient 66 population. Liquids and/or soft foods that are shown not to alter performance of the drug 67
candidates.context: There are many commercial drug product dosage forms such as granules, pellets, powders, or 53 tablets for which the drug product labeling includes instructions for the optional use of soft foods 54 or liquids as vehicles for their administration. 55 5 See guidance for industry Food-Effect Bioavailability and Fed Bioequivalence Studies and guidance for industry Bioavailability and Bioequivalence Studies Submitted in NDAs or INDS-General Considerations.

candidates.statement: Only those liquids and/or soft foods demonstrated to have no appreciable effect on drug product 103 performance should be proposed as vehicles. The potential impact of a vehicle on drug product 104 performance is determined by assessment of drug product quality attributes, including potency 105 (assay), in vitro dissolution/release, and other pertinent attributes when the drug product is used 106 with the proposed vehicle(s). In section IV, standardized in vitro methods for evaluating 107 compatibility of the proposed liquid and/or soft food are described. 108

candidates.statement: In the subsequent sections of this document, an “intact” drug product refers to solid oral dosage 110 forms such as granules, pellets, powders, as well as certain specific modified release drug 111 products such as coated mini-tablets or beads that are labeled to be administered via sprinkling 112 (e.g., capsules or packets containing beads). 9 When a drug product requires handling to make it 113 suitable for administration in a vehicle, such as crushing a tablet, emptying capsule contents, 114 making serial dilutions, or mixing syrup into a vehicle, the resultant product is referred to as a 115 “manipulated” drug product in this document. If critical manipulations are needed, such as 116 emptying capsule contents or crushing a tablet to mix with the vehicle for ease of administration, 117 the impact of the manipulations should be studied. The preparation and use instructions provided 118 in labeling should give clear instructions that can be followed by the patient, caregiver, or 119 healthcare professional in a homecare setting or a healthcare facility. 10
candidates.context: 8 Refer to the following: http://www.fda.gov/Drugs/EmergencyPreparedness/BioterrorismandDrugPreparedness/ucm130996.htm and http://www.fda.gov/Drugs/EmergencyPreparedness/BioterrorismandDrugPreparedness/ucm063814.htm . The following are key considerations and recommendations for selection and use of vehicles for 122 drug product administration and are intended to ensure that any liquid or soft food proposed as a 123 vehicle does not compromise drug product performance. 124

candidates.statement: Using liquids and soft foods as vehicles for drug administration can prove to be challenging 128 because many factors such as seasonal, regional and climate conditions can influence the 129 composition of natural food substances. Liquids and soft foods that have relatively small 130 fluctuations in their composition and characteristics (such as sugar content, acidity, viscosity) 131 may be better candidates for screening as potentially compatible liquids and/or soft foods with 132 drug products for further testing. Liquids and/or soft foods should be screened with consideration 133 of the following characteristics: 1) the drug substance, 2) the drug product, 3) the properties of 134 the proposed vehicle, such as its acidity/alkalinity and binding/chelating characteristics, and 4) 135 the target population. For liquid dosage forms, composition of the drug product (including use of 136 stabilizing, emulsifying, and suspending agents) should be considered when selecting possible 137 vehicles to mix with the drug product. If possible, sponsors should identify more than one 138 compatible vehicle to provide options for patients with allergy or intolerance to a single vehicle. 139
candidates.context: A. Selection of Liquids and Soft Foods: Compatibility and Suitability 126 For compatibility assessments, the pH value of proposed liquids and soft foods should be 141 considered before further testing for their compatibility with the intact or manipulated drug 142 product, including products with coatings. For example, for drug products with an intact enteric 143 protective coating suitable for an acidic environment with pH values up to pH 5, the proposed 144 vehicle should not have a pH value higher than 5, as exposing the coating to higher pH values 145 will disrupt and remove the coating from the drug product. 11 , 12 See Appendix A for commonly 146 used soft foods and liquids with their approximate pH ranges. 147

candidates.statement: It is important that a comprehensive suitability determination is performed to evaluate potential 149 use of the proposed vehicle in the targeted patient population. Suitability determinations should 150 include a composite assessment of multiple factors, such as the patient’s medical condition; 151 perceptions of the product-vehicle mixture such as flavor, texture, and mouthfeel; and age- 152 related responses to physical characteristics of the mixture. For example, perception of mouthfeel 153 of the intact or manipulated drug product in the vehicle mixture will vary with the targeted 154 patient population. Graininess of the drug product and vehicle mixture can trigger chewing in 155 young patients. 156
candidates.context: 12 Jurecki ER, Cunningham A, Mahoney JJ, Tingley D, Chung S, James N, Cohen-Pfeffer JL, 2014, Sapropterin Dihydrochloride Mixed with Common Foods and Beverages, Top Clin Nutr, 29 (4), 325-331. If a certain liquid or soft food is considered unsuitable for the targeted patient population, even if 158 the proposed vehicle(s) and the intact or manipulated drug product are chemically compatible, 159 the indicated soft food or liquid may not be considered an acceptable vehicle for use. For 160 example, adding a drug product to applesauce or another soft food is inappropriate if the targeted 161 patient population is infants who are not yet eating solid food. Such data, when available, for 162 liquids and soft foods evaluated and found to be unacceptable should also be submitted, 163 including the rationale for avoiding their use as vehicles. 164

candidates.statement: A direct assessment of the impact of the proposed vehicle on the intact or manipulated drug 168 product should be conducted to determine the compatibility of the proposed vehicle with the 169 drug product. Specifically, a liquid or soft food is considered suitable for use as a vehicle for 170 drug product administration when it has no appreciable effect on drug product stability or 171 performance. The resulting drug product-vehicle mixture should exhibit no change in potency (as 172 determined by assay) over the proposed use time period and no significant change in drug release 173 characteristics. See section IV for recommended methods. 174
candidates.context: B. Impact of Vehicle on the Drug Product 166 Once combined, the drug product and vehicle mixture should be ingested immediately (or as 176 directed in the labeling) to avoid dosing errors or inadvertent dosing, and inadvertent 177 contamination of the drug product-vehicle mixture. When the labeling calls for immediate use of 178 the mixture, such use should be adequately supported by product quality assessments that are 179 carried out at pre-determined times over two hours after preparation of the mixture. The two- 180 hour assessment period is considered to provide the necessary time window to ensure physical 181 and chemical stability of the drug product-vehicle mixture. Microbiological testing is not needed 182 for the drug product-vehicle mixture if it is intended to be used within two hours because the risk 183 of microbial proliferation to harmful levels is miminal. candidates.statement: Acceptance of the drug product is determined in part by palatability and swallowability that 195 would determine the patient adherence. Palatability is defined as the quality of a drug product 196 that makes it pleasant or acceptable in terms of taste, after-taste, smell, and texture and is a 197 critical factor in determining patient acceptance of oral dosage forms. Swallowability may be 198 defined as the patient being able to take the drug without gagging or choking. Taste sensation 199 develops early in life and evolves with age. In general, the goal should be to develop drug 200 formulations with a neutral taste that would be acceptable to the majority of patients. Although 201 taste-masking technology is advancing rapidly, for those drug products where taste-masking is 202 not possible, alternate approaches such as mixing with appropriate liquids and/or soft foods to 203 mask taste can be employed to improve palatability of a finished dosage form. In cases where the 204 drug substance dissolves in the vehicle, the drug product and vehicle mixture should be 205 adequately taste-masked, if necessary for palatability. 206

Therefore, the palatability and swallowability of the drug product mixed with the 213 vehicle should be determined in the intended population of use. 214

Even with functionally scored tablets, there are limitations in accurately dividing a tablet 238 into dose strengths beyond that provided by the scoring. 17 For example, we recommend against 239 dividing nonfunctionally scored tablets into smaller doses (such as one-fourth of a tablet), 240 because it can result in crumbling of the tablet and inaccuracy of the recommended dose. candidates.statement: The suggested volume of the vehicle for mixing with solid oral dosage forms should take into 247 consideration the age, size, and average consumption of the vehicle by the targeted patient 248 population. For example, children younger than two years old may not be able or willing to 249 ingest large volumes of liquids or soft foods at one time, whereas this volume may be acceptable 250 for an older child or adult. To ensure administration of the full dose of the drug and to facilitate 251 swallowing, the smallest volume of vehicle(s) sufficient to provide acceptable taste-masking, 252 roughly 5 to 15 mL, should be used to prepare the drug product and vehicle mixture. In addition, 253 homogeneous (i.e., uniform) mixing of the drug product in a smaller volume of vehicle is 254 generally easier and will facilitate complete administration of the dose. If the homogeneous 255 mixing of the intact or manipulated drug product with a small volume of the vehicle is difficult 256 and requires a large volume (e.g., more than 15 mL) of the vehicle for dosing, exploring alternate 257 vehicles should be considered to avoid incomplete dosing if all of the drug product and vehicle 258 mixture cannot be readily ingested. 259
candidates.context: 2. Dose and Dosing Volume 245 E. Drug Product and Vehicle Mixtures for Repeated Use or Multiple Users 261

candidates.statement: Generally, use of vehicles for drug administration refers to single use of the preparation where 263 the drug product, once mixed with the liquid or soft food, is consumed immediately by a single 264 patient. Under certain circumstances, use of the drug product-vehicle mixture preparation for 265 multiple doses (e.g., one or more patients) can be considered acceptable (i.e., in a healthcare 266 facility or in another setting where qualified professionals are responsible for preparing the drug 267 product-vehicle mixtures and dosing the patients). Adequate characterization of the drug product 268 and vehicle mixture (including adequate in-use stability data and microbiological assessments), 269 and instructions for preparing the drug product-vehicle mixture, should be included in the 270 submission to support such multiple dose labeling statements. 271

candidates.statement: In cases where the drug product labeling describes feeding tube administration, orally 277 administered drug products can be given through a feeding tube (oral or enteral) to pediatric or 278 adult patients who are unable to ingest solid or liquid dosage forms. 18 In addition to the 279 recommended assessments in this guidance, the feasibility and risk of administration of the drug 280 product-vehicle mixture through a feeding tube should be addressed. For example, if the product 281 may be administered by feeding tube, then an assessment demonstrating delivery of full volume 282 of the mixture with no loss of drug product or potency is necessary, and should include the 283 volume of solution to be used to rinse the feeding tube to ensure complete administration of the 284 mixture. Similarly, factors that can result in the risk of drug aspiration or blockage of the tube 285 should be evaluated. 286

candidates.statement: Integrity: A qualified vehicle should be shown to maintain the drug substance quality attributes. 405 If the drug product has a coating and is used intact, the qualified vehicle should have no impact 406 on the coating and as a result, on the integrity of the drug substance within the drug product. In 407 the cases where a coated tablet is to be crushed before mixing and the integrity of the coated 408 tablet is intentionally compromised, or where the drug product dissolves in the vehicle, exposing 409 the drug substance, the potential for the proposed vehicle to impact the integrity of the drug 410 substance (e.g., changes in polymorphic form, loss of bead integrity) should be evaluated. 411

candidates.statement: Stability: Stability assessment of the drug product-vehicle mixture should be provided to 429 support labeling instructions for its preparation and labeled use time. To qualify a vehicle for 430 immediate drug administration, a two hour stability assessment (USP controlled room 431 temperature: 20º C-25º C) 26 should be conducted in a manner consistent with immediate use of 432 the mixture as described in the labeling. Additionally, stability assessment under refrigerated 433 conditions (USP controlled cold temperature: 2º C-8º C) may be needed. 434

candidates.statement: Homogeneity (dose uniformity): The proposed vehicle(s) should also be suitable for 444 preparation of homogeneous mixtures. The drug product should be thoroughly mixed with the 445 liquid or soft food to ensure a homogeneous mixture. Even though the drug product and vehicle 446 mixture is prepared for immediate use, it is possible that the patient may not ingest all of the 447 mixture immediately. In such cases, the more homogeneous the mixture is, the more reliable the 448 estimate of the ingested dose. To evaluate the homogeneity of the mixture, the drug product and 449 vehicle mixture should be divided into equal portions (n=3 to 6) and tested. 450

candidates.statement: Composition of soft foods or liquids such as added thickeners, sweetening agents, and other 454 ingredients can alter release and delivery of drug substance from the drug product. 27 In cases 455 where the drug substance is not immediately dissolved in the liquid or soft food, dissolution/ 456 release testing of drug substance from the dosage form mixed with the proposed vehicle should 457 be carried out according to established methods. 28 Dissolution testing should be conducted in 458 media typically used for testing solid oral dosage forms and USP Apparatus I or Apparatus II can 459 be used. The following dissolution media are generally recommended: (1) 0.1 N HCl or 460 simulated gastric fluid USP without enzymes; (2) USP buffer at pH 4.5; (3) USP buffer at pH 6.8 461 or simulated intestinal fluid USP with or without enzymes; and (4) FFESSGF. 29 , 30 The sample 462 preparation process should enable assessment of drug dissolution/release patterns for the drug 463 product-vehicle mixture in a manner consistent with drug dissolution/release characteristics and 464 claims for the drug product. 465
candidates.context: 3. Dissolution/Drug Release Testing 452 Typically, 12 individual units of the dosage form are used for dissolution testing of a drug 467 product. This information should be included in the vehicle qualification report or cross- 468 referenced to the drug product information in the submission. For dissolution/release testing of 469 drug substance from the drug product-vehicle mixture, data from six units mixed into the 470 proposed vehicle should be collected at each pre-determined sampling time. A comparison of the 471 dissolution profile for the original product with the drug product mixed with the proposed 472 vehicle should meet the similarity factor (f2) acceptance criteria. 31

candidates.statement: The following examples illustrate labeling text for the DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION 532 section for drug products (as is or in a manipulated form) that can be mixed with liquids or soft 533 foods. The labeling should include specific use information, such as the volume and temperature 534 of the qualified vehicle(s) approved for use. 535
candidates.context: Examples of Labeling Language 530 • Drug X capsules should be swallowed intact with a glass of water. For patients with 537 swallowing difficulties, Drug X capsules can be opened and the contents sprinkled onto 538 a teaspoon (5 mL) or tablespoon (15 mL) of soft food and ingested immediately. Use 539 only foods that do not require chewing, such as apricot, banana, or sweet potato baby 540 food; applesauce; and instant pudding. Contact of the capsule contents with foods such 541 as milk, custard, ice cream, and many other dairy products can dissolve the protective 542 (or enteric) coating and destroy the drug substance. 543
